fatal_errors: The proposed comparison holds elemental composition fixed while changing atomic-size mismatch, but atomic-size mismatch is principally determined by the identities and fractions of the constituent elements; the stated intervention is therefore not operationally realizable without introducing another variable.

The claimed causal link from greater atomic-size mismatch to enhanced grain-boundary diffusion is asserted without direct supporting evidence and is not established by the cited phase-formation criterion.
The experiment does not test the target surface-energy-driven Au/Cu segregation mechanism in sub-10 nm AuCoCuNiPt particles.
explanation: The hypothesis addresses high-temperature diffusion, segregation, and instability in high-entropy nanoalloys, so it has broad problem alignment and acknowledges that configurational entropy need not prevent kinetic degradation. However, it does not reconstruct the relevant material, heating protocol, or mechanism. It substitutes grain-boundary diffusion driven by atomic-size mismatch for surface-energy-driven Au/Cu surface segregation coupled to particle reshaping, melting, and evaporation. Its predicted demixing and coarsening also differ from the observed disappearance of 2–4 nm particles, Au/Cu loss, particle shrinkage, size-distribution widening, and elliptical-to-spherical evolution. The proposed conditions—prolonged annealing above 1000 °C in inert gas—are far from stepped heating to 973 K in vacuum and may introduce different degradation regimes. Although TEM-EDX, XRD, and grain-size measurements provide a nominal falsification test, the central independent variable cannot be changed while retaining identical composition. E1 supplies only general extreme-environment motivation, while E2 indicates that atomic-size difference can correlate with bulk HEA phase formation; neither supports accelerated grain-boundary diffusion in nanoalloys. Thus this is not a well-supported alternative mechanism.
